howToUse: This script bank is a ready-to-use set of seventeen self-coaching prompts and perspective-shift scripts — one to three sentences each — written specifically for the moment your brain stalls and convinces you that you simply aren't wired for this. Keep this document open alongside whatever you're writing. When you hit a stuck moment, find the script that matches it, read it aloud or write it out, and get back to the page. No journaling, no processing — just a fast redirect so you keep moving.
promise: These seventeen scripts hand you the exact words to dissolve the "my brain doesn't write" conviction the moment it surfaces, mapped to three specific stuck moments: the blank page, the rewrite loop, and the post-publish spiral. Pull the script that fits the moment and keep going.

tools.name: The 17-Script Reframe Bank
tools.instructions: Find the stuck moment below that matches where you are right now. Read the script aloud or type it out. Move on.
tools.content:
# The 17-Script Reframe Bank

Scripts are grouped by the three stuck moments coaches report most. Find yours. Use it.

---

## STUCK MOMENT A — THE BLANK PAGE
*The document is open. Nothing is happening. The cursor is blinking.*

**Script A1**
I don't need the right sentence — I need any sentence. Every word I type is raw material, and raw material can be shaped; a blank page cannot.

**Script A2**
Right now I am not writing copy. I am talking to one person about something they already feel but haven't found words for yet. I've done this on calls. I'm doing it now.

**Script A3**
The blank page doesn't mean I have nothing to say. It means I haven't started saying it yet. I'll write the version only I would write, and fix it later.

**Script A4**
If a client said this exact thing to me in a session, what would I say back? I'll write that. That's the opening.

**Script A5**
The copy I'm avoiding writing is not better than the copy I'm about to write. It doesn't exist yet. Mine will.

**Script A6**
I know what my client is feeling the moment before they book a call. I'll write from that moment. That's not a writing skill — that's pattern recognition I already have from doing this work.

---

## STUCK MOMENT B — THE REWRITE LOOP
*You've rewritten the same sentence, paragraph, or section more than three times and it keeps getting worse or feels less like you each time.*

**Script B1**
I am not in a writing problem. I am in an evaluation problem. I'm using judging-brain when I need making-brain. I'll stop evaluating and just write forward.

**Script B2**
The version I'm trying to get to is a feeling, not a sentence. I can't edit my way to a feeling — I can only write toward it. I'll write three completely different versions and choose from there.

**Script B3**
This sentence has been rewritten so many times that I can no longer hear it. I'll read the whole paragraph aloud and mark only what sounds like me.

**Script B4**
I don't need this sentence to be perfect — I need it to be mine. A sentence that sounds like me and is slightly clunky beats a polished sentence that sounds like anyone.

**Script B5**
I'm editing to remove myself from this copy. Every time I change it, I'm making it safer and less specific. Safer is what kills conversion. I'll put the original version back.

**Script B6**
The person who will book from this page won't notice the sentence I'm stuck on. They'll feel the paragraph it sits inside. I'll zoom out and read the paragraph.

---

## STUCK MOMENT C — THE POST-PUBLISH SPIRAL
*You've hit publish or send, and now you're convinced it was wrong, embarrassing, or proof you can't do this.*

**Script C1**
The copy is out. The feeling I have right now is not feedback — it's exposure discomfort. Exposure discomfort means the copy was specific enough to be mine. That's correct.

**Script C2**
The worst-case version of this scenario is that the copy doesn't convert. That's data, not failure. Data tells me exactly what to adjust next time. I'm collecting data.

**Script C3**
I have never heard a client say 'I didn't book because the copy wasn't polished enough.' I've heard clients say 'something you wrote made me feel like you already knew me.' That's the bar. Not perfection.

**Script C4**
If I sent that email to my best client and they read it, what would they think? They would think it sounds like me. That's the point.

**Script C5**
The copy I just published is better than the copy that doesn't exist because I never published it. I shipped. That is the skill being built here.

---

> **How to build the habit:** Screenshot or copy the two or three scripts that match your most common stuck moment. Paste them at the top of your working document before every writing session so they're already there when you need them.

tools.name: The Stuck-Moment Matcher
tools.instructions: Fill this in once before your next writing session — it maps your specific stuck pattern to the scripts that will work hardest for you.
tools.content:
# The Stuck-Moment Matcher
*A one-page worksheet — five prompts — that identifies which scripts in the bank belong at the top of your working document.*

---

**PROMPT 1 — Your Most Common Stuck Moment**
Of the three stuck moments in the script bank (blank page / rewrite loop / post-publish spiral), which one shows up most for you?

> My most common stuck moment: **[BLANK PAGE / REWRITE LOOP / POST-PUBLISH SPIRAL]**

---

**PROMPT 2 — What You Tell Yourself**
Write out, in your own words, the exact thought that appears when you hit that moment. Don't tidy it up — write it the way it actually sounds in your head.

> "[THE EXACT THOUGHT — e.g. 'I'm not a writer, this is going to be terrible, everyone will be able to tell']"

---

**PROMPT 3 — What That Thought Makes You Do**
What's the first behaviour that follows that thought? (Check a different tab, go make coffee, start a new document, delete everything, etc.)

> When that thought appears, I immediately: **[THE AVOIDANCE BEHAVIOUR]**

---

**PROMPT 4 — The Three Scripts That Counter It**
Look at the scripts in your most common stuck moment group. Which three feel like the most direct counter to the thought you wrote in Prompt 2?

> Script 1: **[SCRIPT CODE — e.g. A2]** — because **[ONE SENTENCE ON WHY IT WORKS FOR YOU]**

> Script 2: **[SCRIPT CODE]** — because **[ONE SENTENCE ON WHY IT WORKS FOR YOU]**

> Script 3: **[SCRIPT CODE]** — because **[ONE SENTENCE ON WHY IT WORKS FOR YOU]**

---

**PROMPT 5 — Your Personal Redirect**
Using the language of your three chosen scripts, write a single redirect sentence in your own voice — the one you'll read first when the stuck moment appears. Make it sound like you talking to yourself, not like a stranger wrote it.

> My personal redirect: **"[YOUR SENTENCE]"**

---

**What to do with this worksheet:**
Paste your three script codes and your personal redirect sentence at the very top of every new document you write inside the programme. The barrier isn't knowledge — it's the gap between reading a module and opening a blank document. This sheet closes that gap before you open the document.

tools.name: The Discovery-Call-to-Copy Transfer SOP
tools.instructions: Run this five-step process before you write any section of a sales page or email — it converts the language you already use on calls into the raw material for the copy.
tools.content:
# The Discovery-Call-to-Copy Transfer SOP
*Five steps. Use before writing any new section.*

---

**What this SOP is based on:**
The conviction that you can't write is almost never about writing. It's about the distance between talking and typing. On a discovery call, you locate the exact sentence a prospect is holding — the one they can't finish — and you finish it for them. That's the Client Psychology Reverse-Map in action: you work backwards from the specific moment a coaching buyer ran out of their own answer, not from the general category of pain they're in. This SOP makes that same move in writing, so the copy you produce is structurally built from the psychology you already understand, not from a template you're filling in from the outside.

---

**STEP 1 — Name the section you're about to write**

Before you open a blank document, write down exactly which section or email you're writing. One thing only.

> I am writing: **[SECTION NAME — e.g. "Hero section of my signature programme sales page" / "Subject line and opening paragraph of the re-engagement email"]**

---

**STEP 2 — Recall the call moment, not the category**

Think of a real discovery call where something shifted. Not the general problem the client had — the specific moment. The mid-sentence stop. The thing they said that told you they'd run out of their own answer.

Write it here as they said it, or as close as you can get:

> "[THE EXACT OR NEAR-EXACT THING THEY SAID — e.g. 'I know what I should be doing, I just can't seem to make myself do it — and I don't know if that's a strategy problem or a me problem']"

---

**STEP 3 — Write what you said back**

What did you say at that moment? Not the full session — just the first thing out of your mouth that made them exhale. Write it the way you said it, not the way you'd write it.

> I said: **"[YOUR EXACT RESPONSE — e.g. 'That's not a you problem. That's a missing structure problem, and structure is fixable']"

---

**STEP 4 — Transfer directly to the section**

What you said in Step 3 is your opening. Not a draft of your opening — the opening. The prospect reading your sales page is in the same mid-sentence stop as the client on that call. Paste Step 3 into your document and write the next sentence from there.

If it sounds too casual for a sales page, leave it. Casual and specific converts. Polished and general does not.

---

**STEP 5 — Run the one-question test**

After writing your section, ask yourself one question only:

> **"If my best client read this, would they think 'yes, that's exactly it' or would they think 'that could be about anyone'?"**

- If the answer is **'exactly it'** — move to the next section.
- If the answer is **'anyone'** — return to Step 2 and find a more specific call moment.

---

> **Note on the SOP:** Steps 2 and 3 take the most time on the first use. After three or four uses, the call-moment recall becomes fast because you're building a personal library of the specific moments that do conversion work for your offer.

tools.name: The Pre-Session Writing Checklist
tools.instructions: Run through this eight-item checklist before every writing session — it takes under two minutes and prevents the three conditions that cause the blank-page spiral.
tools.content:
# The Pre-Session Writing Checklist
*Eight items. Run before every writing session.*

---

**SET-UP — before you open a document**

- [ ] I have closed every browser tab that is not directly related to what I am writing
- [ ] I have set a timer for **[YOUR SESSION LENGTH — e.g. 25 / 45 / 60 minutes]** — when it goes off, the session ends regardless of where I am
- [ ] I have put my three personal scripts from the Stuck-Moment Matcher at the top of this document

---

**SCOPE — what this session covers**

- [ ] I have identified the ONE section or ONE email I am writing in this session — not the whole sales page, not the full sequence: **[SECTION NAME]**
- [ ] I know which discovery-call moment I'm pulling from for this section (Step 2 of the Transfer SOP): **[THE MOMENT IN ONE LINE]**

---

**RULES FOR THIS SESSION**

- [ ] This session is production-only. I will not evaluate, judge, or delete what I produce during this session — that is a different session
- [ ] If I get stuck, I will read a script from the bank — I will not open a new tab, ask an AI to write it for me, or stop the session early
- [ ] At the end of this session I will record what I produced: **[WHAT I WROTE — e.g. "Hero section opening, first draft, 140 words"]**

---

> **The rule this checklist enforces:** Production and evaluation are different cognitive modes. This session is production. Evaluation — where you decide if it's good — belongs in a separate session, scheduled separately. A first draft that exists is the material the programme's review and feedback process works with. A draft that was deleted mid-session doesn't exist yet.

nextStep.heading: Put the Scripts to Work in Your Next Module
nextStep.body: The fastest way to get value from this script bank is to use it during the programme, not after it. Before your next module session, fill in the Stuck-Moment Matcher (it's five prompts, takes under ten minutes), then paste your three chosen scripts at the top of whatever document you'll be writing inside that module. The Transfer SOP and the Pre-Session Checklist are there for every live writing session — run the checklist at the start, pull the SOP when you're extracting copy from your call experience. The scripts lose none of their effect the more you use them.
